excerpt: What to do after a Charleston parking lot or garage accident, and why private property complicates the liability question.
keyTakeaways: Most South Carolina rules of the road technically apply only on public roads, but the duty to stop and report a crash and the DUI and reckless-driving laws apply in parking lots too (S.C. Code § 56-5-20), and negligence law applies everywhere. Property owners can be liable for poor lighting, inadequate signage, or dangerous design. Pedestrian strikes in parking areas are common. South Carolina's comparative fault rule bars recovery at 51% or more fault, and the filing deadline is three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), or two years if a government body, such as the city that owns a garage, is the defendant (S.C. Code § 15-78-110).

faqs.question: Who is at fault in a parking lot accident?
faqs.answer: Generally, the driver backing out of a space must yield to vehicles in the travel lane. At intersections within parking lots, drivers are expected to follow the same right-of-way conventions as on public roads, although the traffic statutes themselves technically apply only to public roads. The specific facts determine fault.

faqs.question: Will police respond to a parking lot accident?
faqs.answer: In the City of Charleston, police dispatch an officer to every reported private-property crash, but the officer decides whether to write a formal report. Always call, and if anyone is hurt, South Carolina law requires you to notify police immediately (S.C. Code § 56-5-1260).

faqs.question: Can I sue the parking lot owner?
faqs.answer: Yes, if the parking lot or garage design, maintenance, or lighting contributed to the accident. Premises liability claims can be brought against property owners for hazards like poor visibility, confusing traffic flow, and inadequate lighting.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a claim?
faqs.answer: Three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), but two years if a government body, such as the city that owns a garage, is the defendant (S.C. Code § 15-78-110). Two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33).

faqs.question: What if I was partially at fault?
faqs.answer: SC allows recovery if your fault is less than 51 percent.

faqs.question: Are parking garage accidents different from parking lot accidents?
faqs.answer: Parking garages present additional hazards including blind corners, steep ramps, low ceilings, poor lighting, and pedestrians walking between parked cars in enclosed spaces. The garage owner owes customers reasonable care, and in a structure with these hazards, reasonable care demands more: lighting, mirrors, signage and maintenance.
